pois.name: Mellon Institute columns
pois.altText: Front of the Mellon Institute: a long row of tall, smooth stone columns.

prompt.text: This building has a row of giant stone columns. How many pieces make up one?

reveal.text: None stacked. Each column is a single piece of stone.

story.text: Each of the 62 columns here is one solid piece of Indiana limestone, about 60 tons.
When the Mellon Institute opened in 1937, they were the largest monolithic columns in the world.
The building, now part of Carnegie Mellon, reaches six stories underground to bedrock, to keep lab experiments steady.

pois.name: Dippy the dinosaur
pois.altText: A life-size dinosaur with a long curved neck, standing on a lawn beside the museum.

prompt.text: A long-necked dinosaur stands on the museum lawn. Is it bone, or something else?

story.text: This is Dippy, a fiberglass copy of a Diplodocus installed in 1999, 100 years after Andrew Carnegie funded the dig that found the original.
The first bone, a toe, was found in Wyoming on July 4, 1899, earning it the nickname 'the star-spangled dinosaur.'
The real skeleton still stands inside, and Carnegie gave casts to museums in London, Paris, and other cities.

pois.name: “A Song to Nature” fountain
pois.altText: A stone fountain with a wide round basin and bronze figures in the center.

prompt.text: Water spouts into the fountain’s basin from all around its rim. What’s spouting it?

reveal.text: Turtles. Four bronze turtles spout water into the basin.

story.text: This 1918 fountain honors Mary Schenley, who donated the land for Schenley Park.
The figures show Humanity playing a lyre to Pan, the earth god.
Its sculptor, Victor David Brenner, also designed the Lincoln penny, so you've probably carried his work in your pocket.

pois.name: Forbes Field wall
pois.altText: An old red brick wall with large white numbers painted on it.

prompt.text: This red brick wall has big white numbers on it. What do you think they measure?

reveal.text: Distances from home plate: 457 and 436 feet.

story.text: This wall is all that's left of the outfield of Forbes Field, home of the Pittsburgh Pirates from 1909 to 1970, and of the Negro League Homestead Grays.
Bill Mazeroski's ninth-inning home run here won the 1960 World Series. Fans still gather at this wall every October 13 to relive it.
Home plate from the last game is preserved in the lobby of Posvar Hall, just across the street.

done.text: Walk complete. Check your phone for your field journal.

cue.text: Start at Fifth Avenue and Bellefield.
Head down Bellefield to Forbes Avenue.
Cross Forbes toward Schenley Plaza and the Frick Fine Arts Building.
Follow Roberto Clemente Drive to the old brick wall by Mazeroski Field.
